coach_says: You're already in a tough spot, and Ne2 doesn't change much, but notice what it leaves alone: your rook on c1 sits on the long diagonal of Black's bishop on h6, with only the queen on g5 in between. After Nf3+ and Qf6 the queen steps aside and the bishop takes the rook. Nd5 heading for e3 blocks that diagonal, or Rc2 just steps off it. When an enemy queen and bishop line up on your piece, look at what happens if the front one moves.

Nd5 is the best move here. It adds a second attacker to the pinned knight on f6 and puts your knight on a strong central square, so Black can't easily untangle. This is exactly how to follow up an attack on a broken king position: bring more pieces to the pinned piece.
also: pile up on the pinned piece

coach_says: Qh3 is fine. Your queen on h5 was attacked by the g6 pawn and you found a safe square that still keeps an eye on e6. Qe2 was very slightly better because it guards e6 more directly and stays closer to home, but the difference is tiny.

You were in check and Rf2 is a perfectly good way out, about as good as moving the king. The one move to avoid was Qf2, which lets the knight jump to h3 with check and win material. Things were already difficult, and this block didn't make them worse.

Castling long here is reasonable: it gets your king away from the rook on g7 and brings a rook to d8 to guard the d7 pawn. Other moves were about as good. You're down material, so the job now is to stay solid and look for chances.
This endgame was already very hard to hold, and a5 is about as good as anything else. Your bishop moves were equally fine. Nothing here to change.

Your queen needed to move, and you're still better after Qg6, but on g6 it can be chased by Nf4 at once. Qe4 puts the queen in the centre where it attacks the knight on e2 and adds a second attacker to the d4 pawn alongside your bishop on b6, so White is busy defending instead of chasing you. When you move an attacked queen, prefer a square that creates threats over one where it will be kicked again.

White has pushed g4 and f3 with the king still in the centre, which loosens their position. The classic answer to an attack on the wing is to hit back in the centre: c5 attacks d4 right away and starts opening lines while White's king is stuck on e1. c6 is a solid move but too slow, it gives White time to finish developing. When your opponent lunges with flank pawns, look for a central pawn break.
concept: meet a wing attack in the centre

coach_says: Qh4 puts your queen on the same diagonal as Black's queen on e7, with only the rook on f6 in between. Black trades rooks on f1 with check, the f6 rook leaves that diagonal, and you have to recapture instead of saving your queen, so Qxh4 wins it. Simply Rxf6 first would have kept your extra pawn. Before moving your queen, check whether an enemy piece could move out of the way and uncover an attack on it, especially with check.

Your rook on d5 was attacked by the bishop on c4, and Nc2 ignores that. White just takes Bxd5, and if you grab the rook on a1 with the knight, the bishop takes e4 and your knight is stuck in the corner. Rc5 saves the rook and attacks the bishop at the same time. Before making your own threat, check what your opponent is already attacking.

Count the pieces on e5: Black attacks it with the knights on d7 and c6 and the bishop on g7, three times, and you defend it only with the knight on f3 and bishop on f4. After castling, Black takes on e5, trades queens and wins the pawn. Qe2 adds a third defender down the e-file and keeps the pawn. Whenever you have an advanced pawn, count attackers and defenders before making a quiet move.

Your rook on f5 is out in front with few safe squares, and after dxe5 dxe5 White plays g4 to kick it; you end up giving the rook for the knight on f3. The engine's g4 pushes first: it attacks the f3 knight and takes away White's g4 idea. When you put a rook out in front of your pawns, ask whether a pawn push could chase it with nowhere good to go.

Nd7 lets White trade the bishop for your knight, and the pawn ending that follows is lost: after Bxd7 Kxd7 White's king walks to h6 and the kingside pawns run, while your king is far away on the queenside. Your knight was your winning piece; Nb3 or Ne6 keeps it and heads for d4. Before allowing a trade into a king and pawn ending, count which king reaches the pawns first.
concept: trading into a lost pawn ending
also: king too far from the action

coach_says: Your rook on f1 was attacked by the bishop on a6, and Rxf7 gives it up for just one pawn with no follow-up, since the king simply takes it. The calm d3 blocks the bishop's diagonal and opens the way for your c1 bishop at the same time. When a piece is attacked, look for a developing move that blocks the attack before throwing the piece in.
also: block the attack with a developing move

coach_says: Taking the bishop on c4 lets White play Rd8+. After Bf8, Bh6 threatens Rxf8 mate and you can't stop it, because your c8 bishop blocks your own rook from defending the back rank and your knight is now too far away to help. Bg4 was the move: it attacks the rook and gets the bishop off c8 so your rook guards d8. Before grabbing material, check your back rank when your king has no escape square.

You could have taken the bishop on b3 for free. It looks protected by the a2 pawn, but that pawn is pinned: if it recaptures, your rook on a8 gives check down the open a-file, which is illegal. So Qxb3 just wins a piece. When a piece seems defended, check whether the defender is pinned to the king.

Your bishop on e4 was attacked twice and d5 defends it, but White just trades the knight for it and you're left with a weak pawn on e4 that the rook can attack. Retreating with Bb7 keeps your strong bishop on the long diagonal pointing at g2, and you stay clearly better with the open a-file and your c-pawn. When your good piece is attacked, think about whether defending it just invites a trade that helps your opponent.

White's queen on c7 is deep in your camp with almost no squares, and you could have trapped it. After e5 every queen move lands on a square you control, since e5 also opens your f8 bishop's diagonal to d6, and Ne8 next attacks it, so White has to give the queen for a knight. Bg4 lets the queen escape with Qxb7. When an enemy queen goes raiding, count its escape squares and look for a move that takes the last ones away.

Ng5 moves the same knight twice and attacks f7, which is only guarded by the king but isn't really in danger because nothing else of yours joins in. Meanwhile you're still a pawn down: Nxd4 takes it back and develops at the same time. Black can simply chase the knight back with Be7 or h6. In the opening, win back material and develop new pieces before starting one-piece attacks.

Your knight on e5 was attacked by the knight on d7 and had no defender, so it had to do something. Nc6 hits the queen but sends the knight deep into Black's camp where it can get stranded after Qc5. Simpler was Nxd7, trading it off, or Qf3 keeping pressure on the long diagonal. A one-move threat is only good if your piece is safe and useful on its new square afterwards.
